blocks.content: Subduction zones are destructive plate boundaries where lithospheric plates sink into the mantle, giving rise to deep ocean trenches, powerful earthquakes, and explosive volcanism.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Subduction zones form at convergent boundaries where a denser lithospheric plate sinks beneath a less dense plate into the Earth's mantle.
Oceanic-continental convergence produces continental volcanic arcs like the Andes, whereas oceanic-oceanic convergence forms island arcs like Japan and the Aleutians.
The dipping zone of earthquake foci along the sinking slab is known as the Wadati-Benioff zone, extending up to 700 km into the Earth.
Subduction zones balance the generation of new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges by recycling older lithosphere back into the mantle.
Continental crust cannot subduct into the mantle due to its low density and high buoyancy.

rows: Older, cooler, and denser oceanic plate
Dense oceanic plate under less dense continental plate
Regional and contact metamorphism along continental margin

items: Distinguish clearly between Island Arcs (Oceanic-Oceanic convergence) and Volcanic Arcs (Oceanic-Continental convergence) for geography Prelims.
Deep-focus earthquakes (>300 km depth) occur exclusively along the Wadati-Benioff zones of subduction boundaries.
Remember that oceanic lithosphere subducts because it cools, thickens, and becomes denser than the underlying asthenosphere as it moves away from mid-ocean ridges.
